intro.en: The suffixes and prefixes that add size, affection, contempt or intensity to a word.

ahorita.nota: Very common in Mexico and Central America.

texto.en:
**Diminutives.** The main one is **-ito / -ita**: casa → **casita**; libro → **librito**; poco → **poquito**; cerca → **cerquita**. Words ending in **-e**, **-n** or **-r**, and short words, take **-cito** or **-ecito**: café → **cafecito**; joven → **jovencito**; pueblo → **pueblecito**; flor → **florecita**.

Spelling follows the sound: po**c**o → po**qu**ito; ami**g**o → ami**gu**ito.

A diminutive rarely means only small. It adds affection (**abuelita**), softens a request (**¿Me esperas un momentito?**), or makes something sound unimportant (**un problemilla**). Other endings: **-illo** (chico → **chiquillo**) and **-ín** (pequeño → **pequeñín**).

Names take them too, and so do adverbs: **Carlitos**, **Anita**; **ahorita**, **despacito**, **tempranito**.

**Augmentatives.**

- **-ón / -ona**: big, or doing something a lot. **Un sillón** was once a big silla. **Un comilón** eats a lot; **un dormilón** sleeps a lot.
- **-azo**: big and impressive (**un cochazo**, **un golazo**), or a blow given with something (**un portazo**, **un golpazo**, **un codazo**).
- **-ote**: big and a bit clumsy (**grandote**, **un librote**).

Careful: **-ón** changes the gender of some words: **la** silla, **el** sillón; **la** película, **el** peliculón.

**Contempt.** **-ucho** and **-ucha**: **una casucha**, **feúcho**, **un cuartucho**.

**Intensifying prefixes.** Colloquial: **super-** (superbién, superguapo) and **requete-** (requetebién). More formal: **archi-** (archiconocido) and **ultra-**.

**Words that are no longer diminutives.** Some have become independent: **la mesilla** (bedside table), **el bolsillo** (pocket), **la ventanilla** (ticket window), **el cigarrillo**, **el pañuelo**.

frases.es: Pasa, hijo, siéntate en el sillón. ¿Te hago un cafecito?
frases.en: Come in, dear, sit in the armchair. Shall I make you a little coffee?

frases.es: Vale, abuelita, pero solo un poquito, que tengo prisa.
frases.en: OK, Granny, but just a little bit, I'm in a hurry.

frases.es: ¡Siempre con prisa! Espera un momentito, que te he guardado unas rosquillas.
frases.en: Always in a hurry! Wait just a moment: I've kept some doughnuts for you.

frases.es: Eres un sol. Por cierto, ¿has visto el cochazo que se ha comprado el vecino?
frases.en: You're an angel. By the way, have you seen the flashy car the neighbour has bought?
analisis: que se ha comprado el vecino

frases.es: Lo he visto y lo he oído. Anoche dio un portazo que despertó a todo el barrio.
frases.en: I've seen it and heard it. Last night he slammed the door so hard it woke the whole neighbourhood.
analisis: Lo he visto y lo he oído

frases.es: Pues vive en una casucha. No lo entiendo.
frases.en: And yet he lives in a hovel. I don't understand it.

pregunta.en: Complete with the diminutive of poco.

poquito.en: The c becomes qu to keep the sound.

the slam of a door.en: The suffix -azo can mean a blow.

a big door.en: Here -azo is a blow, not size.

peliculón.en: La película becomes el peliculón: masculine.

peliculona.en: With -ón the word becomes masculine: el peliculón.

peliculita.en: That would be a little film.

pregunta.en: ¿Me esperas un momentito? Why the diminutive?

It softens the request.en: It makes it sound like less trouble.

The moment is very short.en: It is about politeness, not time.

explicacion.en: -ón here means someone who does it a lot.
Dormilón: someone who sleeps a lot.
Words ending in a stressed vowel usually take -cito. In Spain you also hear cafelito.

bloques.frase: Espera un momentito, que ahora vuelvo

traduccion.en: Wait just a moment, I'll be right back.

texto.en:
**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (150–180 words).** Write a dialogue between a grandmother and her grandchild full of diminutives, and a complaint full of augmentatives.

**Speak (about 3 minutes).** Tell an anecdote aloud twice: once neutrally and once with affectionate and exaggerated suffixes.
